fine_trace.note: Attacker-controlled raw JSON string bytes (including the 5-byte pseudo-UTF-8 sequences 0xF8 0x81 0x80 0x80 0x80 inside the "s" value) are referenced directly from the fuzzer input buffer; these bytes are never validated as proper UTF-8.
The raw string length is computed (5 bytes per 5-byte pseudo-UTF-8 char); this same (data, size) pair is later passed to escapeString, so the 5-byte sequences survive deserialization verbatim.

fine_trace.code: auto result = unescapeString(data, size, errorCode, errorPosition);
fine_trace.note: unescapeString copies the raw bytes into an oatpp::String without any UTF-8 validation, preserving the 5-byte sequences as the stored string content.
The tree string node holding the malicious bytes becomes the value of DTO field Test1::s, so the bytes are carried into the subsequent serialization round-trip.
The stored string is fed into escaping with the default escapeFlags = FLAG_ESCAPE_ALL (includes FLAG_ESCAPE_UTF8CHAR), so every byte >= 0x80 is escaped via escapeUtf8Char.

fine_trace.code: v_buff_size escapedSize = calcEscapedStringSize(data, size, safeSize, flags);
fine_trace.note: calcEscapedStringSize computes the output buffer size from the UTF-8 sequence byte length (charSize): 5/6-byte sequences get 11 bytes per char, but the actual escape output length depends on the decoded code point, not charSize.

fine_trace.code: result += 11; // '\u+FFFFFFFF' - 11 chars NOT JSON standard case
fine_trace.note: ROOT CAUSE: for charSize 5/6 only 11 bytes are reserved per char, while escapeUtf8Char emits the 12-byte surrogate-pair form '\uXXXX\uXXXX' whenever the decoded code point is in [0x10000, 0x200000) (e.g. code 0x40000 for bytes F8 81 80 80 80). The per-char reservation is 1 byte short, so the allocated buffer is undersized.
A heap std::string of exactly escapedSize bytes is allocated (11 bytes per 5-byte char); this is the buffer that escapeUtf8Char will write past.

escapeUtf8Char returns 12 for each 5-byte char with code < 0x200000, while only 11 bytes were reserved per char, so pos advances beyond the allocated region and the write runs off the end of resultData.

SINK: writeUInt16 performs a 4-byte store at buffer[8..11]; the buffer holds only 11 bytes (indices 0..10), so index 11 is out of bounds. ASan confirms: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE at Hex.cpp:41 called from this line.
